newsitem.title: USA: Oil profits fuel record U.S. Gulf lease sale.
newsitem.headline: Oil profits fuel record U.S. Gulf lease sale.

text.p: Oil and natural gas companies, flush with cash from last year's strong profits, on Wednesday shattered bidding records in the latest federal auction of Gulf of Mexico drilling rights.
A standing room only crowd packed a downtown New Orleans hotel ballroom as a record 1,790 bids for rights to drill in federal waters off the coast of Louisiana were unsealed.
At day's end, producers had anted up a total $1.24 billion, making the sale the most active in terms of dollars bid since 1985.

Shell Offshore Inc., a unit of Royal Dutch/Shell Group, led the field with 191 bids, including 120 high bids totalling $71.75 million, according to the U.S. Minerals Management Service, which regulates offshore drilling in federal waters.
"Those people that said the Gulf was a dead sea not so long ago I think were wrong," said Bob Armstrong, an Interior Department assistant secretary.
The high bid in the day-long auction was $8.05 million submitted jointly on a Mississippi Canyon tract south of the Mississippi River delta by Kerr-McGee Corp. and Agip Petroleum Co.

In the lease sale, considered a barometer of the health of the domestic oil and gas industry, producers submit sealed bids on rights to drill on available tracts in the Gulf. Additional payments, known as royalties, are also paid on oil and gas produced from the leaseholdings.

A lower royalty rate on deepwater tracts sparked active bidding in waters 400 meters (1,312 feet) or deeper, with producers bidding on 587 tracts eligible for royalty relief. The lower royalties have led to three straight record-breaking lease rounds.
Before unsealing the first of the bids, MMS Regional Director Chris Oynes donned a red sport coat -- a tradition last seen in the "big money" auctions during the boom years in the early 1980s.
"It looks like we are going to have a lot of money (today)," Oynes said, drawing cheers from producers left flush with cash from strong oil and gas prices and record profits last year.

With many of the shallower tracts leased out under five-year contracts, producers will be scrambling for available rigs and crews, investment banker Matt Simmons, president of Houston- based Simmons & Co., said.
"It's going to be tough. You're going to have to start building new rigs," Simmons said. "This industry needs to start expanding like crazy in its capacity."
